toxic-attraction.brief: The type they are magnetically drawn to that always ends the same way. Name the pattern, never a person. The reader should feel caught, not insulted.

you: Your {singular}, your toxic attraction
The type you keep choosing, based on {your} {singular}
her: Why {her} taste keeps breaking {her} heart, based on {her} {singular}
him: The woman he keeps choosing and the one he actually needs

toxic-attraction.pattern: Section 1 opens "You attract people who [misread one of your good traits as a flaw]", runs 2-3 short sentences of how that plays out, then a line where the universe or the world keeps handing you the wrong version of what you want, then a flat 4-6 word correction. Section 2 opens "Someone [three adjectives]" or "Someone who [does the right thing]", then a sentence starting "A partner who", then closes on an explicit contrast: you do not need X, you need Y.
toxic-attraction.patternNote: The thing that gets misread in section 1 must be a GOOD trait, never a flaw - spontaneity read as inability to commit, calm read as something to borrow, depth read as entertainment. That misreading is the whole angle; if section 1 describes a bad habit instead, the post has failed. The closing contrast in section 2 must name the wrong thing and the right thing in the same breath, not just state a want. Written for the you voice; mirror every pronoun for her and him.
examples: Your Toxic Attraction: You attract people who see you as a project they never plan to finish. They love that you point out their flaws and work to fix them while they make excuses. You fall for potential like it has a deadline. You keep thinking if you just organize the situation well enough, it will finally make sense. It will not.

Your Toxic Attraction: You attract people who fall in love with your peace and slowly disturb it. They are drawn to your calm like it is something they can borrow. You create balance wherever you go and keep attracting people who throw it off. The universe keeps sending you chaos with good manners. They never learn to be steady back.

Your Toxic Attraction: You attract people who flirt like it is therapy and disappear the moment things get real. They are fascinated by your depth right up until it asks something of them. The world keeps sending you puddles and calling them oceans. They run the second the mystery turns into intimacy.

What You Really Need: Someone who can handle the full weight of who you are without flinching. A partner who goes beneath the surface willingly and stays there. You do not need someone fascinated by your depth. You need someone brave enough to live in it.

What You Really Need: Someone spontaneous, funny, and emotionally grounded. A partner who can keep up with your energy and still be someone you come home to. You do not need more chaos. You need a person who understands that freedom and foundation are not opposites.

What You Really Need: Someone organized, honest, and already emotionally grown. A partner who says what they mean and does what they say. You do not need to manage a person. You need to be met by one.

the-love-lesson.brief: One corrective lesson about love, delivered as a verdict and then a route out of it. Section one names what they have wrong and why; section two is the specific admission that starts the repair. Tough, then warm - never scolding.

you: The love lesson you need to learn, based on your {singular}
Your {singular}, your love lesson
What you still have wrong about love, by your {singular}

the-love-lesson.pattern: Section 1 opens with a flat aphorism that denies a belief they hold ("Love is not a salary"), then 3-4 very short sentences naming the behaviour, then the fixed phrase "You need to learn that" plus the correction, then closes on 2-3 fragments. Section 2 opens with the fixed phrase "It starts with admitting" plus what they will not admit, then a sentence beginning "Somewhere" that locates where they learned it, then a direct instruction to do one specific thing, then closes by reframing what they thought they were doing.
the-love-lesson.patternNote: Both fixed openings are mandatory and must appear word for word - "You need to learn that" in section 1 and "It starts with admitting" at the very start of section 2. The instruction near the end of section 2 must be one concrete act a person could do this week (say a sentence out loud, show someone the flaw), never "be vulnerable". The rhythm is the device: long observation, then three or four words. A strong closing move is "You were never X. You were Y" - use it, but not on every item.
examples: Your Lesson: Love is not a salary. You cannot work hard enough to deserve it. You provide, you build, you show up with results instead of feelings. You need to learn that the people who love you don't want your output. They want your presence. Your softness. The part of you that isn't producing anything. That part exists. You've just never let it out of the office.

Your Lesson: You cannot test someone into being trustworthy. You watch. You probe. You set little traps and wait for people to fail them. You need to learn that trust is not a verdict you reach after enough evidence. It's a risk you take before you have any. No one can prove themselves to a judge who's already decided everyone eventually lies.

Your Lesson: Peace you have to purchase with silence is not peace. You smooth things over. You agree. You shrink your needs until they fit in your pocket. You need to learn that a relationship without your honest voice in it is not a relationship. It's a performance of one. Conflict doesn't end love. Avoiding it does. Slowly. Politely. Completely.

Your Healing: It starts with admitting whose voice is grading you. It was never yours. Someone taught you that love had conditions. That you were almost enough, if you just fixed one more thing. So you've been fixing ever since. But there is no finish line. There never was. Show someone the flaw you always hide. Let them see it and stay. You were never broken. You were just measured by someone who didn't know how to love.

Your Healing: It starts with admitting when you learned to disappear. Somewhere, being easy kept you safe. Your needs caused problems, so you folded them smaller until even you couldn't find them. Now you're loved by many and known by no one. Say the true thing sitting in your throat right now. Your voice will shake. Let it. You were never keeping the peace. You were keeping yourself hostage.

Your Healing: It starts with admitting what the tests are protecting. Somewhere, you trusted completely and it destroyed you. So you swore it would never happen again. Tell someone one guarded truth. Let them hold it. And when they do, let it count. Put the armor down. You survived once. You might not have to again.

your-danger.brief: The exact condition under which they stop being safe to cross, and then the same capability seen as something worth loving. Cold first, warm second, no apology in either direction.

you: Your {singular}, your danger
What makes you dangerous, based on your {singular}
What each {singular} is like with nothing left to prove

your-danger.pattern: Section 1 names the exact condition under which they become dangerous, gives 3-4 short sentences of what they do in that state, then closes on a flat line that raises the stakes instead of softening them. Section 2 concedes the cold behaviour and why it happens, pivots in the middle on a single But or Yet, then closes on the specific good thing they give when they feel safe.
your-danger.patternNote: The danger is never villainy - it is a good trait with the safety off: ambition fuelled by humiliation, patience that becomes quiet erasure, insight that becomes knowing exactly what someone needs to hear. Section 2 MUST contain a But or Yet turn in the middle; without it the section is just a compliment. The trait in section 2 has to be the SAME trait as section 1 - if section 1 is about going cold, section 2 cannot arrive at generosity out of nowhere. Section 1 never apologises, section 2 never scolds.
examples: Your danger: You become most dangerous when someone thinks they can break your spirit. Pain doesn't always slow you down. Sometimes it gives you direction. You turn humiliation into ambition, rejection into fuel, anger into action. People fear your temper. They should fear what comes after it.

Your danger: You understand how people think faster than they realize you're studying them. You hear contradictions. You notice what someone avoids. You can change your tone, your argument and your entire approach in seconds. You don't only know what to say. You know what the other person needs to hear.

Your truth: You can stay attached long after something has stopped making you happy, because letting go feels like destroying a life you already built in your head. But that same attachment makes you someone's stability. You stay consistent, you remember what matters, and you create the kind of loyalty people spend years searching for.

Your truth: You can act untouchable when being overlooked has wounded you more than criticism ever could. Yet when you feel truly loved, you become incredibly generous. You celebrate your people loudly, defend them fiercely, and have a gift for making someone feel special simply because they're yours.

why-people-fall-for-you.brief: What draws people in, then the self-protective habit that drives the same people out. The two halves must be the same person, described twice.

you: Your {singular}, why people fall for you
Why people fall for you and why they lose you, by your {singular}
What each {singular} is loved for and left for

why-people-fall-for-you.pattern: Section 1 opens with a short flat claim about what they are like, unpacks it for 3-4 sentences, then closes on a sentence containing the exact words "People fall for" followed by two or three things stacked with commas. Section 2 names the self-protective habit, unpacks what it costs, then closes on a sentence containing the exact words "People lose you because" followed by the real reason.
why-people-fall-for-you.patternNote: Both closing phrases are mandatory and word for word - "People fall for" in section 1, "People lose you because" in section 2. The reason in section 2 must be a self-deception the reader half knows: a habit they call by a flattering name. Name both names in the same breath - walls disguised as strength, one foot out the door called freedom when it was fear of being tied to a single life. Section 2 is never about the other person failing, always about the reader's own exit.
examples: Why people fall for you: You see people. Not the version they perform, the one underneath they thought no one noticed. You make others feel understood in a way that almost aches. People fall for your tenderness, the way you turn heavy moments soft, the way loving you feels like being forgiven for things you never confessed.

Why people fall for you: Being with you feels like living more. You pull people into experiences they would never have chased alone, and the world looks brighter through your eyes. People fall for your appetite for life, the comfort of your presence, the way you make even ordinary days feel worth remembering.

Why people lose you: You confuse control with love, and you hold on so tightly that people start to feel managed instead of held. You struggle to let anyone see you unsure or unravelling, so they never feel fully let in. People lose you because you built walls disguised as strength. You wanted closeness but couldn't stand to be seen as anything less than solid.

emotions-you-dont-express.brief: The feeling they swallow, the one underneath it, and the thing they have wanted for years and never once asked for out loud.

you: Your {singular} and the emotions you don't express
What each {singular} buries instead of saying
Your {singular}, your unspoken need

emotions-you-dont-express.pattern: THREE sections, each with a different fixed opening shape. Section 1 opens with ONE abstract noun and a full stop - Resentment. Insecurity. Anxiety. - then unpacks it and closes on a short flat line. Section 2 opens with a gerund phrase and a full stop - Feeling abandoned. Feeling not good enough. - then unpacks it and closes on a short flat line. Section 3 is three or four clauses each beginning "To be" or "To have", separated by full stops, and nothing else.
emotions-you-dont-express.patternNote: The three openings must stay in that order and must never swap shapes: single noun, then gerund, then stacked infinitives. Section 3 has NO closing commentary - the stacked wants ARE the ending, and one sentence added after them kills the whole post. Section 3 is why this gets saved, so every clause must be something the reader has wanted for years and never asked for. Section 2 is not a restatement of section 1: section 1 is the emotion they feel, section 2 is the older fear underneath it.
examples: The Emotion You Bury: Resentment. You feel everything and carry everyone. You give until you're empty and then you give more. And sometimes it turns bitter and you never say it. You just go quiet and pull back into your shell.

The Emotion You Bury: Insecurity. You walk in like you own the room. Inside you're wondering if they'd still love you dimmed. You perform confidence because you learned the crowd leaves when the light goes out. No one knows how much you question yourself.

The Feeling You Hide: Feeling abandoned. You nurture people who never nurture back. You remember every time you needed someone and the space stayed empty. You stop asking. You just keep caring from a safer distance.

The Feeling You Hide: Feeling not good enough. You give your best and still replay what you missed. You criticize yourself harder than anyone else ever could. Nothing you do feels finished. Nothing feels like enough.
The Need You Never Voice: To be adored for your heart, not just your spark. To be seen on the days you're low. To be loved when you're not performing.
The Need You Never Voice: To be told you're enough without having to be perfect. To rest without guilt chasing you. To be loved for who you are, not who you're trying to become.

your-dark-gift.brief: One trait that damages people, stated without flinching, then the identical trait as the reason someone will never get over them. Same quality, two readings.

you: Your {singular}, your dark gift
The gift that costs people something, by your {singular}
What each {singular} does to people without meaning to

your-dark-gift.pattern: Section 1 states the flaw as a capability - something they DO to people, never something wrong with them - unpacks the cost over 3-4 sentences, then closes on the most damning line in the post. Section 2 MUST open with the word But, reframes the identical trait as the thing that makes them worth loving, then names the partner who unlocks it with a phrase beginning "With someone" or "With a partner", and closes on the trait turning.
your-dark-gift.patternNote: Section 2 opening with But is mandatory and is the hinge of the format. The trait must be IDENTICAL across both sections, not a related virtue - the one who burns people is also the most alive person you will ever meet, the one who cannot let go also loves deeper than anyone. A strong closing move is "stops being a wound and becomes" something - use it, but not on every item. Section 1 must not hedge and section 2 must not apologise for section 1.
examples: Your dark gift: You set people on fire and walk away before the flame dies. You burn bright, then go cold, chasing the spark of the beginning and losing interest the second it settles. You leave people still burning long after you've moved on, remembered forever by hearts you never stayed to hold. You crave the chase more than the catch.

Your light: But that same steadiness makes you the most reliable love a person could find. When someone finally deserves your patience, they get a devotion nothing can shake. With a partner who stays as steadily as you do, your loyalty stops being a wound and becomes the foundation you both stand on for life.

Your light: But a heart that forgets nothing loves harder and deeper than anyone alive. When the right person chooses you back, being loved by you feels like being finally, fully seen. With someone who stays without being held in place, your memory stops being a wound and becomes the thing that makes them feel unforgettable.

your-secret-desire.brief: What they actually want in love, escalating from the abstract wish to the concrete need to one specific scene they have imagined and never said aloud.

you: Your {singular}, your secret desire
What each {singular} secretly wants in love
The thing you want and never ask for, by your {singular}

your-secret-desire.pattern: THREE sections that escalate. Section 1 opens with an infinitive - "To be chosen first, always" or "To feel completely safe with someone" - then "You want someone who" plus what that looks like. Section 2 names the need as a bare noun phrase, then "You need someone who" or "You need to be" plus the specific reassurance. Section 3 is stacked noun phrases and images with NO "you" subject at all - a scene, not a sentence.
your-secret-desire.patternNote: The escalation is the format: abstract wish, then concrete need, then one specific imagined moment. Section 3 dropping the "you" subject entirely is what makes it read as a confession rather than a description - "Someone grabbing your face mid-argument and kissing you hard. Passion that matches your fire." If section 3 starts using full you-sentences it collapses into section 2. Desire and Need must not restate each other: the desire is what they want to be, the need is what they require to believe it.
examples: Secret Desire: To be chosen first, always. You want someone who picks you without hesitation, who fights for you like you fight for everything else. You crave being someone's priority, their first thought, their instant yes.

Secret Desire: To feel completely safe with someone. You want love that feels like coming home. Someone who protects your heart like it's made of glass and never makes you question if you're too much.
Secret Need: Emotional security you can count on. You need someone who stays when things get hard, who doesn't run when you cry, who makes you feel like you're their person no matter what.
Secret Need: Constant validation that you're still special. You need to be told you're beautiful, amazing, irreplaceable. Compliments aren't vanity for you - they're how you know you're loved.

Secret Fantasy: Someone grabbing your face mid-argument and kissing you hard. Passion that matches your fire. Love that feels like a battle you both want to win. Intensity that never fades into comfortable routine.
Secret Fantasy: Grand romantic gestures that everyone sees. Public declarations of love. Someone who's proud to be with you and wants the whole world to know they're yours and they're the lucky one.

your-silence.brief: The sentence they never say, and then the exact words to say instead. Ends by handing the reader something short enough to actually use.

you: Your {singular}, your silence
What each {singular} never says out loud
The sentence you swallow, based on your {singular}

your-silence.pattern: Section 1 opens "You never say" or "You never admit" plus the exact thing they will not say, then 2-3 sentences of what it costs to hold it in, then closes on how it looks to everyone else. Section 2 denies the belief that made silence necessary, names who has earned the truth, then gives the reader an actual SENTENCE to say - five words or fewer, plain - and closes on what saying it would be worth.
your-silence.patternNote: The handed-over sentence is the entire point of the angle and is mandatory: "Say I'm exhausted to someone safe." "Say the sentence you swallow every time." "Say this was hard and I need it noticed." It must be short enough to repeat from memory and must never be "be vulnerable", "open up" or any therapy phrasing. Section 1 never suggests the silence was stupid - it was protective and it worked, which is why it is hard to drop.
examples: Your silence: You never say I need you. You'd rather handle it bleeding than let someone watch you struggle. Every time you wanted to reach out, you talked yourself out of it and carried the weight alone. People think you're fine because you never let them see otherwise.

Your silence: You never say how much it took. You carry weight no one acknowledges, work harder than anyone notices, push through pain while smiling like it's nothing. You're terrified that if you complain, you'll seem weak, so you stay quiet and let the effort go unseen.

Your voice: You don't have to earn love by being impressive. The people worth keeping want the off-stage you, the tired one, the one who isn't performing anything. Say I'm exhausted to someone safe. The relief of being human in front of one person is worth more than the whole audience.

your-sin.brief: One named moral failing, stated as a vice rather than a quirk, then the release from whatever story made it feel necessary.

you: Your {singular}, your sin
The sin each {singular} keeps committing
What you are actually guilty of, by your {singular}

your-sin.pattern: Section 1 opens with ONE word naming the sin followed by a full stop, then immediately qualifies it so it is precise rather than cartoonish ("Not lies exactly, but charm."), then 2-3 sentences of how it actually operates, then closes on the cost stated flatly. Section 2 removes the obligation that justified it, reframes what they were really doing, then closes on a plain truth that lands as relief.
your-sin.patternNote: The sin must be a real vice named in one word - Deceit, Martyrdom, Ego, Envy, Pride - never a soft euphemism like "overthinking". The qualifier right after it is what keeps it fair: the deceit is charm, the martyrdom is giving that keeps score. Section 2 is never forgiveness handed down from above; it cancels a duty the reader invented for themselves. Distinct from emotions-you-dont-express, which also opens on a single word: there the word is an EMOTION they feel, here it is a FAILING they commit.
examples: Your sin: Deceit. Not lies exactly, but charm. You know exactly what to say to make people trust you, open up, adore you, and you use it before you even mean to. You perform closeness so well that people think they know you. They know the character you play.

Your sin: Ego. You need to be seen so badly that being ordinary feels like dying. Every room, you're subtly performing, subtly measuring whether you're still the one they're watching. The applause feeds you for a second, then leaves you hungrier than before.

Your salvation: Nobody asked you to disappear for them. Pouring yourself out isn't noble if it leaves you bitter and hollow. The most loving thing you can do is fill your own cup first, so what you give comes from overflow, not from a wound that wants to be seen.

how-she-loves-how-she-leaves.brief: Her love described in full, then her exit described in full. The leaving is slow, warned, and finished internally long before it happens out loud.

her: How she loves and how she leaves, by her {singular}
Her {singular}, her way of loving and leaving
What each {singular} woman is like in love

how-she-loves-how-she-leaves.pattern: FULL sentences throughout, nearly every one opening "She" or "Her". Section 1 runs 4-5 sentences building how she loves and closes on a summary claim about the love itself ("Her love is impossible to ignore"). Section 2 opens by denying the obvious exit ("She doesn't leave after the first mistake"), traces the slow accumulation that changed her mind, and closes on the leaving already being complete before it happened.
how-she-loves-how-she-leaves.patternNote: This is the her-voice sibling of how-you-love-how-you-leave and must NOT copy its device: that angle opens both sections on a bare fragment, this one uses full subject-verb sentences only. Never make her impulsive or cruel - she forgives, she warns, she gives chances, and she leaves only once staying costs more than going. Section 2 closes on the gap between emotional and physical departure ("by the time she leaves physically, she left emotionally months ago") or on her choosing herself. Do NOT open section 1 with the words "She loves" - the label already says How She Loves and echoing it wastes the strongest position in the paragraph. Open on the verb that is specific to her instead: She throws, She builds, She creates, She offers, She guards. Every item in the carousel must use a different one.
examples: How She Loves: She loves with intensity and zero apology. She won't make you guess how she feels. If she chooses you, she'll stand proudly beside you and push you to become your best self. She's fiercely protective and never hesitates to fight for the relationship. Her love is bold, genuine, and fully alive.

How She Loves: She loves with pride, passion, and unwavering loyalty. She wants you to feel admired and celebrated every single day. She'll hype your dreams, defend you in your absence, and make you feel like the luckiest person alive. She believes love should be shown, not hidden. Her love is impossible to ignore.

How She Leaves: She stays longer than most people think. She'll forgive, overlook flaws, and hope things improve because she doesn't give up easily. But every broken promise chips away at her trust. One day, without much warning, she accepts she's holding on to something that no longer feels healthy. She won't leave dramatically. By the time she leaves physically, she left emotionally months ago.

How She Leaves: She doesn't leave impulsively. She analyzes, reflects, and gives countless chances before making a final decision. She'll tell you what's hurting her and hope things improve. But if nothing changes, she slowly begins detaching. The overthinking eventually turns into acceptance. By the time she walks away, she's already made peace with losing the relationship.

you: Your {singular}, your addiction
What you are actually addicted to in love

Your {singular}, your self-sabotage

You are somebody's red flag. Here is which one.

you: The same relationship you keep having, based on {your} {singular}

you: How you test people without telling them
The test each {singular} sets and never announces

you: How you go cold, based on {your} {singular}

you: What you put up with that you should not
Your {singular}, your blind spot in love
her: What {she} calls patience and everyone else calls settling

how-they-lose-interest.brief: The fade. Not the dramatic ending — the quiet one. What stops first, what they keep doing out of guilt, and the moment they knew.

you: How you lose interest, based on {your} {singular}
him: How he checks out before he leaves
her: How {she} leaves months before {she} goes

deepest-fear.brief: The fear underneath the personality — the one that explains the behaviour. Pair it with the strength that grew out of the same root.

you: Your {singular}, your fear
The fear you never say out loud

deepest-fear.pattern: Section 1 opens with a bare noun phrase naming the fear and no verb ("Being underestimated."), then 3-4 sentences of evidence all starting "You", then closes on a sentence beginning "You're scared of" or "You're terrified of" that states the specific outcome they dread. Section 2 opens with a declarative "You [verb]" claim of the strength, then 3-4 sentences of proof, then closes on one short flat claim that settles it.
deepest-fear.patternNote: The power in section 2 must be the SAME trait as the fear in section 1 seen from the other side - fear of being overlooked pairs with commanding attention, fear of failing silently pairs with perfectionism that makes them irreplaceable. If the two sections name unrelated things the post has failed. Section 1 must open on a fragment, never a full sentence; that clipped opening is the format. No comfort in section 1 and no hedging in section 2.
examples: Your fear: Being underestimated. You act strong but deep down, you want people to see just how serious your dreams are. You're tired of being the one everyone overlooks, the one whose ambitions get dismissed as cute or unrealistic. You're scared of being stuck in a life where nobody takes you seriously.

Your fear: Living a life that feels small. Routine scares you more than chaos ever could. You're terrified of becoming someone who just goes through the motions, waking up to the same day on repeat until suddenly you're old and realize you never actually lived. Predictability feels like prison, and you're scared you'll get trapped there.

Your fear: Never figuring it out. You feel like you're running out of time to become who you're meant to be. Everyone else seems to have their path mapped out while you're still searching for the starting line. You're scared that you'll spend your whole life feeling like you're on the verge of something without ever actually arriving.

Your power: You perfect everything you touch. Your attention to detail, your work ethic, your refusal to do anything halfway makes you irreplaceable. You don't just complete tasks, you elevate them. People rely on you because you're the one who actually follows through. Your standards aren't punishment, they're proof of your excellence.

Your power: You transform through fire. Every breakdown became a breakthrough. Every loss taught you something nobody could have taught you in comfort. You don't fear the dark because you've lived there and walked out stronger. You rise from things that would destroy other people.

Your power: You breathe life into everything. Your need for balance, beauty, and meaning transforms ordinary moments into experiences people remember forever. You don't settle for surface level anything. You pull magic out of the mundane. Your presence makes everything more vibrant.

core-wound.brief: The original injury, described through its symptoms rather than its story. Then the specific thing that heals it. Tender, not clinical.

you: Your {singular}, your wound
Who you become after heartbreak, based on {your} {singular}

Your blind spot, based on {your} {singular}

never-say-out-loud.brief: Sentences they have thought and never said. Write them as the actual unspoken line, first person, so each bullet reads like something overheard.

you: What you never say out loud, based on {your} {singular}
her: What {she} never says out loud
The things {she} has never told you

never-say-out-loud.pattern: [A single admission, first person, that costs them pride to say.]
never-say-out-loud.patternNote: One sentence, no second clause explaining it. This is the raw confession alone - the restraint is the device. If a line needs a because-clause to land, it is the wrong line. Distinct from your-truth, which pairs armor with truth; here there is no armor, only the admission.
examples: I check if you are typing more often than I will ever admit.
I have rehearsed this conversation forty times.
I noticed the exact day you stopped trying.
I would come back if you asked properly.
I am not over it and I have stopped pretending to myself.

you: How you grieve a person, based on {your} {singular}
her: What {she} does after {she} loses someone

you: What is actually tiring you out, based on {your} {singular}
her: The job nobody gave {her} that {she} does anyway

why-underestimated.brief: The trait that gets read as weakness and is not. Name the misreading precisely, then flip it without gloating.

you: Why people underestimate you, based on {your} {singular}
her: Why they always underestimate {her}

what-they-hide.brief: The gap between how they present and what is actually happening. One line for the surface, one for underneath.

you: What you hide well, based on {your} {singular}
her: What {she} is hiding behind being fine
him: What he is hiding behind being calm

what-they-hide.pattern: On the outside [what everyone sees]. Underneath [what is actually happening].
what-they-hide.patternNote: Explicit two-part contrast every line. The outside must be genuinely convincing - a persona people believe, not a thin disguise. The underneath must be plain and undramatic. If the outside is obviously fake, there is nothing hidden and no line.
examples: On the outside the most organised person you know. Underneath one cancelled plan from falling apart.
On the outside endlessly patient. Underneath keeping a list they will never read out.
On the outside the one who checks on everyone. Underneath nobody has asked them in months.
On the outside completely over it. Underneath still checking if you looked.
On the outside the calm one. Underneath the only one who never got to panic.

falling-in-love.brief: The tells. What changes in them the moment it becomes real — outwardly, then underneath, then the fear that comes with it and the one thing that would settle it.
falling-in-love.pattern: FOUR sections. "On the outside" describes observable behaviour in 3-4 short sentences and signs off with a line that names the sign itself. "On the inside" gives the private contradiction in present tense, opening "They're". "Their biggest fear" is exactly two sentences, the first a bare fragment. "Their biggest need" opens "Someone who" or "Someone [adjective] enough to" and closes on a conditional that names the sign again.
falling-in-love.patternNote: The outside and the inside must contradict - warm and public on the outside, nervous and private underneath. This is one of only two angles allowed to name the sign inside the copy, and ONLY in the sign-off lines of sections 1 and 4: "Virgo doesn't flirt. Virgo helps." or "Once Cancer feels safe, they never leave first." Everywhere else use they/them. The fear is about being seen, never about losing the person. Sections get shorter as they go: 3-4 sentences, then 3, then 2, then 2.
examples: On the outside: They start fixing things. Your schedule, your headache, that problem you mentioned once two weeks ago. Virgo doesn't flirt. Virgo helps.
On the outside: Warmer than ever. They compliment you in front of people, pull you into their world, make you feel like the main character. Leo falling in love looks like sunlight.
On the inside: They knew weeks ago. They're just waiting for a sign it's safe to show you. Cancer never falls slowly, they just reveal it slowly.
On the inside: They're weighing it constantly. Is this real, is this right, is this the person. They see every side of everything, including every way this could go wrong.
Their biggest fear: Choosing wrong. Committing fully and then meeting the person they were supposed to wait for.
Their biggest fear: Being fully seen and found flawed. They notice every one of their own imperfections and assume you will too.
Their biggest need: Someone patient enough to earn their trust and gentle enough to keep it. Once Cancer feels safe, they never leave first.
Their biggest need: Someone who notices the small things they do, because that's where they hide all the love they don't say out loud.

the-archetype.pattern: She [does a specific behaviour], [but/until/so a turn reveals what it costs or hides]. The final TWO lines are fixed: second-to-last is "She needs a man who [does the right thing] before she [asks/admits/breaks]", and the last is a defence: "She is not [the label people use], she is just [the real reason]".
the-archetype.patternNote: Only the closing pair is fixed - every line before it is free, and must be a contrast between an outward behaviour and the private cost or motive behind it. The last line always rebuts a specific unfair label (cold, difficult, too sensitive) and supplies the truer reading. Do not put the partner-instruction last; it sets up the defence, it does not close.
examples: She'll fix her own problems and then yours.
She acts fine so well that even she believes it.
She says "whatever" when she means "fight for me".
She remembers exactly what you said three weeks ago at 2am.
She tests if you can handle her distance before she gives you her closeness.
She needs a man who notices she is tired before she admits it.
She is not cold, she is just been her own safe place too long.
She is not too sensitive, you are just used to women who gave up on feeling.
She is not difficult, she just refuses to shrink.
She'll know you're lying before you finish the sentence.
She'll leave you on read while thinking about you all day.
She needs a man who's interesting enough to keep her present.
He'd rather fix it than talk about it.
He remembers things you forgot you told him.

him: Why he was the one, and you found out too late

one-that-got-away.pattern: Written TO the person who lost her, never about her in the abstract. Section 1 opens "She" plus the invisible work she did, lists three specific things she carried, then names the misreading with "You mistook X for Y" or "you thought it just happened on its own". Section 2 stacks sentences that all begin "She deserved someone who" or "Someone who", three or four of them, then closes on a present-tense line beginning "now" that states what he is living with.
one-that-got-away.patternNote: The regret is never stated as regret - it is produced by listing what she did and then showing he read it as obligation rather than choice. Section 2's stacked "someone who" clauses are the engine; each one should be a thing he specifically failed to do. The closing "now" line is mandatory and always present tense: now nobody is going to hold it together the way she did, now every woman you meet you compare to her. Never let him off, and never insult him either - the flatness is what makes it land. Written for the her voice; mirror every pronoun for him.
examples: Why They Got Away: She held your entire life together and you just assumed that is what women do. She remembered everything, planned everything, showed up for everything. You mistook her loyalty for obligation instead of seeing it as a choice she made every single day.

Why They Got Away: She turned your life into something beautiful and you thought it just happened on its own. The meals, the home, the way everything felt right, that was all her. She built your comfort, your peace, your entire world and you got so used to it you forgot she was the one creating it.

What They Deserved: She deserved someone who loved her back with the same whole chest she gave you. Someone who protected her softness instead of testing it. Someone who understood that a love like that comes once and does not come around again. She believed in who you could be when nobody else did. Now every woman you meet you compare to her and none of them come close.

what-they-deserve.brief: Standards written as permission. EVERY line begins "You deserve" - the repetition is the format. Each one names something specific they have been accepting less than.

what-they-deserve.pattern: You deserve to [something costly or vulnerable] and still [be treated well]. OR: You deserve someone who [does not do the specific bad thing].
what-they-deserve.patternNote: Two shapes, ALTERNATING. Shape A pairs a cost with a kept good outcome using "and still": "lose and still be loved", "be wrong and still be wanted". Shape B names an absence in a person: "someone who does not make you fight to be loved". Run mostly A with B appearing around the fourth line and again at the end - the reference posts close on Shape B two times in three. A trailing correction is a strong variant: "Not just when you are impressive." / "Not the place someone rests between something better." A bare "You deserve to be happy" has neither shape and fails.
examples: You deserve to lose and still be loved.
You deserve to be soft and still be respected. Still be wanted. Still be enough.
You deserve to come second sometimes and not be left for it.
You deserve someone who isn't intimidated by how much you are.
You deserve to want without it being too much want.
You deserve to be wrong and still be wanted.
You deserve someone who doesn't make you fight to be loved.

stay-single-until.brief: The specific person worth waiting for, described by behaviour. Concrete and high-standard without being a fantasy.

you: Stay single until you meet someone like this, based on {your} {singular}

stay-single-until.pattern: Section 1 opens with a gerund or noun fragment naming the compromise they keep accepting, then short stacked fragments, then how they came to believe it was normal. Section 2 opens "The person who" and stacks two or three relative clauses each beginning "Who", then turns to what they have always done for everyone, then what the right person does instead, and closes on a flat imperative or claim.
stay-single-until.patternNote: Section 1 is what they have settled for, described so precisely they recognise the exact room it happened in - never a generic red flag. It is not about a bad partner, it is about the shrinking they did voluntarily. Section 2 never describes an ideal personality, only specific ACTS: notices you went quiet, shows up with the thing you mentioned once, hands you water and asks what the plan is. Close on a short line that gives permission to stop: "Stop dating people who treat your fire like a problem to solve."
examples: Don't settle for: Dimming yourself so someone else feels comfortable. Your whole life people have given you the "you're too much" look. Too loud. Too intense. Too fast. And somewhere along the way you started believing them. You started making yourself smaller at dinner tables and in rooms where you should have been the loudest person there.

Don't settle for: Being wanted for the highlight reel. Everyone loves the show. The confidence. The warmth. You've never had trouble being wanted. The problem is you keep being wanted for the performance and not the person running it.

Wait for: The person who notices you've gone quiet and doesn't let it slide. Who shows up at your door with the thing you mentioned once three weeks ago. Who lets you fall apart without looking at you like you're broken. You've spent your whole life holding everyone. The right person finally holds you. And doesn't let go when you pretend you're fine.

The excuse you have almost convinced yourself of, by {your} {singular}

the-delusion.pattern: Section 1 opens with the excuse itself in quotation marks, written exactly as they say it out loud, then "You say it like a strength" or an equivalent acknowledgement, then 2-3 sentences of the behaviour it licenses, then a but-clause that denies the stated reason without yet giving the real one. Section 2 opens "You're not X, you're Y", then a sentence beginning "Somewhere along the way you learned" that locates where it started, then closes by comparing the easy line to the hard admission, usually with the hard one quoted.
the-delusion.patternNote: The quoted excuse must be a sentence people genuinely say and half believe - "I'm too independent to need anyone", "I just take my time with people" - never a strawman. Section 1 must CONCEDE that the excuse contains something true (you do love your freedom, you have been let down) before pulling it away; the post fails if it reads as an accusation. Section 2's "You're not X, you're Y" is the hinge and the Y must be a fear, not a flaw. End on the two sentences side by side: what is easier to say against what is true.
examples: Your Excuse: "I'm too independent to need anyone." You say it like a strength, and you almost believe it. You keep yourself busy, you move fast, you fill your life so full that there's no room to notice the empty part. You tell people you love your freedom, and you do. But freedom was never the reason you kept everyone at arm's length.

The Truth: You're not taking your time, you're bracing for the moment they leave. You've been let down by people you trusted too soon, so now you make love earn its way in slowly, hoping that if it's slow enough it can't hurt you. But some people get tired of knocking, and you lose them while you're still deciding if it's safe to open the door.

gift-or-curse.pattern: Six labelled bullets in a FIXED order. After each label comes a short PHRASE, never a full sentence - no "You are", no "They". Gift and Curse must be two sides of the same trait.
gift-or-curse.patternNote: The content is compressed: "Silent strength that keeps everyone grounded" not "Your power is that you have silent strength". Gerunds and noun phrases only. Your Gift and Your Curse describe the SAME quality from opposite sides. What Heals You is always another person doing something small and specific.

the-warning-label.brief: A five-beat character report written as a product label - a blunt warning, then what dating them is actually like, the defence mechanism, the breaking point, and what they actually need. Each beat is TWO sentences, not a phrase.
the-warning-label.pattern: Five FIXED labels in order, each followed by exactly TWO sentences. Warning states the core trait bluntly. What To Expect elaborates it with a but-clause. What She Hides reveals the insecurity under the trait from Warning. What Breaks Her is a specific triggering scenario. What She Needs is the corrective, stated as a type of person, not an action. (For the his/her voice, swap every pronoun and label to match - What He Hides, What Breaks Him, etc.)
the-warning-label.patternNote: Every beat must trace back to the SAME core trait named in Warning - this is one character study, not five separate facts. The two sentences per beat are short and plain, never a single long sentence. Written below for the her voice - mirror every pronoun for him.
examples: Warning: She'd rather act than sit in the not-knowing. Will decide how it ends before you do.
What To Expect: She'll go all the way in fast and mean every second of it. She is direct, decisive, the one who says the thing nobody else will.
What She Hides: She isn't actually fearless. She just cannot stand the helpless feeling of waiting, so she takes control of the ending before anyone can hand it to her.
What Breaks Her: Being left waiting on an answer. Wanting someone so much she has to sit still for it.
What She Needs: Someone who reassures her without being asked. Someone steady enough that she does not have to rush to protect herself.

What She Hides: She suspects she's only loved when she's impressive. The confidence is partly a performance she keeps up so no one finds out how much reassurance she actually needs.

What Breaks Her: Giving her whole heart and getting a lukewarm one back. Sensing she has to earn the affection she hands out freely.

the-monthly-profile.brief: A full eight-beat personality dossier for one birth month, moving from surface charm to the private exception underneath, then closing on a quoted line in her own voice. Denser than the-archetype - a profile, not a list of loose recognitions.
the-monthly-profile.pattern: Eight FIXED labels in order, each a SHORT PHRASE (2-6 words), except Her mantra which is a first-person line in quotation marks. Her vibe and Superpower are the surface charm. Downfall names the specific cost of that same charm. In public and In private are an explicit contrast pair - composed, then not. Dating her is an instruction, stated as a short condition. Mood is two states joined by a comma, not a single word. Her mantra is what she would actually say out loud, never a description of her.
the-monthly-profile.patternNote: Downfall must trace back to the trait named in Her vibe/Superpower, not introduce a new flaw. In public and In private must contradict each other sharply - if they read as the same mood, the beat has failed. Her mantra is quoted speech, not a summary ("I do it my way" not "she prefers independence"). Distinct from the-warning-label: labels are fixed at eight not five, most beats are short phrases not two-sentence beats, and it ends on a spoken line rather than a stated need. The examples below are deliberately SCRAMBLED across three different months - never assemble them back into one profile, and never reuse a line. Write eight fresh beats for every month.

why-cant-read-you.brief: The gap between the visible surface reaction and the private, delayed, real one. Every line is a specific act of misreading corrected in the same breath.
why-cant-read-you.pattern: Every bullet: "[seems/looks/appears/acts like] SURFACE but [is actually/has been/still/replays] PRIVATE". No subject named - drop it, exactly like a dictionary definition.
why-cant-read-you.patternNote: The two halves must be genuinely opposed. The surface reading is what a stranger would conclude, the private half is what is actually true and is usually about DURATION, REPETITION, or ABSENCE. Lowercase, no full stop, one clause each side of "but".

the-type-he-is.brief: A clipped read on the type, written like someone listing what they already know about him. Unsentimental, a little amused, entirely accurate. Reads as observation, never as a complaint.
the-type-he-is.pattern: Every bullet OMITS the subject and starts with the verb or adjective: "talks big, but...", "protective until...", "obsessed with...". Each line contains a TURN - but / until / while / except / right before.
the-type-he-is.patternNote: Never begin with He or She - the subject is implied and dropping it is the format. All lowercase, no full stop. Each line pairs an outward behaviour with the thing that undercuts it. Keep them short - most run under 60 characters.

what-you-never-say.brief: The unspoken fear or exhaustion behind a trait everyone praises. Every line follows the same confession structure - a private truth the reader would never say to anyone's face. Often lands on a wish to be cared for rather than to keep proving something.
what-you-never-say.pattern: Every bullet opens "That you" then completes ONE private admission - a fear, a reversal of the visible trait, or a wish. At least one line should be a wish for someone else to take over, phrased as a quoted or near-quoted line.
what-you-never-say.patternNote: Distinct from never-say-out-loud, which is first-person with no fixed opening. Here the anaphora is the whole device. Content should trace one throughline per sign - being the one who fights, who goes first, who chases - and reveal the fear or cost underneath it. A strong closer names what they wish someone else would say or do.

your-romantic-superpower.brief: The mechanics of attraction laid out as a spec sheet - what makes them magnetic, how they love, their signature move, and the one thing that keeps someone hooked despite it all. Reads like a dating profile written by someone who knows too much.
your-romantic-superpower.pattern: Seven FIXED labels in order, each a SHORT PHRASE (2-6 words), never a full sentence. Superpower and Draws You In are the surface. the-hidden-side.brief: The private, vulnerable self behind the public persona - written in the third person, about the sign rather than to the reader. Distinct from what-they-hide (no explicit outside/inside contrast) and never-say-out-loud (no anaphora, third person not first).
the-hidden-side.pattern: Five lines, subject dropped or replaced with "the one who" - vary the opener, do not repeat it every line. Each line names something they carry privately: a fear, a private grief, a mismatch between how they are seen and how they feel. A GOOD but not mandatory closer: a wish for something to be given freely, phrased with "without having to ask/earn/perform for it".
the-hidden-side.patternNote: Openers should vary - some start "The one who...", others start with an adjective ("Soft in a way that..."), others with "Tired of..." or "Wants...". Do not use the same opener twice in one slide. The closing line often but not always lands on an unearned desire - checked across three reference signs, two closed that way and one closed on a frustration statement instead, so do not force it every time.

the-defining-quote.brief: One punchy first-person line that could be their motto, followed by a third-person read on the sign - confident, a little combative, occasionally revealing a contradiction. The quote sets the tone; the bullets prove it.
the-defining-quote.pattern: A one-line first-person QUOTE (returned separately, not a bullet) followed by 6-7 third-person bullets about the sign. Bullets vary in shape - direct statements, "you can try to X, but..." warnings, "if [sign] does X, they will Y" conditionals.
the-defining-quote.patternNote: The quote should sound like something the sign would actually say about themselves, confident and slightly defensive - "I don't have an attitude, I have a personality you can't handle." Bullets name the sign directly in third person (not dropped-subject like the-type-he-is). Mix sentence shapes rather than repeating one structure across all lines.

why-you-pull-away.brief: The mechanics of withdrawal traced through a fixed six-beat arc - trigger, realization, contradiction, core hurt, deepest fear, and finally a permission/standard to close on. Every line matters in this exact order.
why-you-pull-away.pattern: SIX bullets, each a fixed ROLE in order, phrasing may vary: 1) "You pull away when [trigger]." 2) "When you realize [pattern]." 3) "When [feeling], even though [contradicting effort]." 4) "What hurts most is [specific pain]." 5) "Your deepest fear is [core fear]." 6) "But you deserve a partner who [standard]." - line 6 always starts with "But" and is the only line offering something positive.
why-you-pull-away.patternNote: Lines 1-5 build downward into the wound; line 6 is the required turn upward - do not let the arc end on pain. Line 3 always contains a contradiction word ("even though", "but"). Keep each line to one sentence, no elaboration after the colon-less structure shown in the examples.
examples: You pull away when being brave starts to feel like being alone.
When you realize you are always the first to fight, reach, try, and forgive.
When needing someone makes you feel weak, even though you are exhausted from being strong.
What hurts most is feeling like people only love your fire when it warms them, not when it burns.
Your deepest fear is that if you stop chasing, no one will come after you.
But you deserve a partner who makes you feel safe enough to stop proving you are worth staying for.

Your deepest fear is being replaced after giving someone the safest version of you.
But you deserve a partner who chooses you gently, clearly, and repeatedly, even when life gets complicated.

im-a-sign-so.pattern: Every bullet opens "I'm a/an {item} so" then a plain trait admission - a behaviour, preference, or contradiction stated flatly, owned rather than confessed.
im-a-sign-so.patternNote: Tone is confident/defiant, not vulnerable - contrast with thats-why (defiant explanation) and im-fine-but (quiet exhaustion).
